plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 3: Polynomial and Rational Functions
plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a rational function on a coordinate plane and marks the two distinct ways its graph breaks. The horizontal axis is labeled x and ticked at odd values from -3 through 9; the vertical axis is ticked at even values from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid. The teal curve comes in two branches. The left branch enters from the far left almost flat and just above the x-axis, carries a small hollow open circle at x equal to -1 marking a point removed from the graph, then descends through the x-axis at x equal to 1 and drops steeply, running off the bottom of the frame as it approaches x equal to 3. The right branch begins high just to the right of x equal to 3, falls quickly, then levels off toward the right edge near y equal to 1. A red dashed vertical line stands at x equal to 3, labeled below the axis in red as Vertical asymptote at x = 3. A blue annotation at the upper left reads Removable discontinuity at x = -1, with a thin arrow to the open circle. Setting the hollow dot against the dashed line is the contrast being drawn: one break is a single missing point, the other sends the curve toward infinity on both sides.

interactionPlan.concept: A rational function's graph can break in two fundamentally different ways: a removable discontinuity is a single missing point caused by a factor that cancels, while a vertical asymptote is unbounded behavior caused by a factor that does not cancel.
elements: x-axis labeled 'x' with ticks at odd values -3, -1, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
y-axis labeled 'y' with ticks at even values -6, -4, -2, 2, 4, 6
dotted gray background grid
teal left branch of the rational curve (enters near y=1 from far left, passes through open circle at x=-1, crosses x-axis at x=1, plunges to -infinity near x=3)
teal right branch of the rational curve (rises from +infinity just right of x=3, levels off toward y=1 at the right edge)
hollow open circle (white fill, teal outline) at (-1, 0.5) marking the removable discontinuity
red dashed vertical line at x=3 (the vertical asymptote)
blue annotation text 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' at upper left with a thin arrow pointing to the open circle
red annotation text 'Vertical asymptote at x = 3' below the axis near the dashed line
movable trace point on the curve (driven by the x slider) with a live (x, y) readout
factored-form annotation 'f(x) = (x+1)(x-1) / [(x+1)(x-3)]' with the (x+1) factors struck through, shown only in cancelled-factor view

interactions.label: Highlight break
interactions.teaches: Switching the highlight makes the visual contrast explicit: the hole is one isolated missing point on an otherwise continuous branch, whereas the asymptote is a line the curve approaches without bound on both sides

interactions.label: Trace x toward the asymptote
interactions.teaches: Dragging x toward 3 from the right sends y to +infinity and from the left sends y to -infinity, proving the break at x=3 is unbounded (not a single missing value), so it cannot be a removable hole

interactions.label: Show cancelled factor
interactions.teaches: Revealing the factored form shows the (x+1) factor present in both numerator and denominator; cancelling it leaves a continuous simplified curve with exactly one excluded point at x=-1, which is why that break is a hole rather than an asymptote

demo_steps.title: Two ways a graph breaks
demo_steps.narration: The teal curve has two breaks: an open circle at x=-1 (a single missing point) and a red dashed line at x=3 (the curve runs off to infinity). The hole is highlighted first.

demo_steps.title: Trace the asymptote
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider so x approaches 3 from the right, then from the left: the trace point's y-value explodes to +infinity then to -infinity, showing the break at x=3 is unbounded, not a hole.

demo_steps.title: Why the hole is removable
demo_steps.narration: Reveal the factored form: the (x+1) factor cancels top and bottom, leaving a continuous curve with only the single point x=-1 excluded — exactly the open circle, and nothing more.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A factor that cancels from numerator and denominator produces a removable hole (one missing point); a factor that remains only in the denominator produces a vertical asymptote (unbounded behavior).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Standard Cartesian plane with a light dotted gray grid; x ticks at odd integers -3..9, y ticks at even integers -6..6. Draw the rational curve f(x)=(x-1)/(x-3) (with a hole at x=-1, y=0.5) in a saturated teal as two separate branches split at x=3. Mark the hole with a white-filled, teal-outlined open circle at (-1,0.5). Draw a bold red dashed vertical line at x=3 spanning the plot height, with red text 'Vertical asymptote at x = 3' just below the axis. Place blue text 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' in the upper-left with a thin gray arrow to the open circle. The trace point is a small filled dot on the curve following the slider, with a compact (x, y) label that grows large in magnitude near x=3. The cancelled-factor annotation appears near the top center in math styling, striking through both (x+1) factors when toggled on. When 'highlightBreak' selects the hole, brighten/enlarge the open circle and dim the red line; when it selects the asymptote, brighten the red dashed line and dim the circle.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between removable discontinuity and vertical asymptote; the learner switches the highlighted break, the open circle or dashed vertical line brightens, and the contrast between a missing point and unbounded behavior becomes clear.
- Slider for x approaching 3; the learner moves a trace point toward the vertical asymptote from either side, the y-value shoots downward or upward, and it becomes clear why x = 3 is not a removable hole.
- Toggle factor-cancelled view: the learner reveals the cancelled factor that fixes the removable discontinuity at x = -1, keeping the hole in place while showing that only one function value is missing from an otherwise continuous branch.

authoredContext:
Notice that x+1 is a common factor to the numerator and the denominator. The zero of this factor, x=−1, is the location of the removable discontinuity. Notice also that x–3 is not a factor in both the numerator and denominator. The zero of this factor, x=3, is the vertical asymptote. See the figure.

Graph of f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x^2-2x-3) with its vertical asymptote at x=3 and a removable discontinuity at x=-1.
